name: hospitality

attributes.attribute: a duty of king and householder to feed and house guests
a king who fed a bard poorly and lost his power
the purpose of the Celtic guest-feast

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Hospitality was a rite and a duty in Celtic Ireland. The king had to spread the tribe's wealth in endless feasting and open-door hospitality. A king who failed his guests could lose the throne. The half-Fomorian king Bres served a bard a scanty meal, and was forced from his power. Hospitality fell on every person, not the king alone. Each householder opened his door to the needy and the traveler. Those who sat at the crossroads showed they would feed and shelter all. The largesse matched the person's means. A poor man could offer a thin share. A rich man was held to spread a great table. The meat given out followed the rank of the guest. The rule swapped the wealth around, so Celtic guesting was a way of sharing resources.
objective: Document hospitality as the royal and cramped duty of Celtic wealth sharing.
key_results: the king's gift to spread and the fall of the king who denied it.
Describe the shared duty of all to feed guests and travelers.
Define the guest-feast as a form of resource reallocation.
